doc.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Singers, records and Jammin' the Blues
title: Records versus live sets: Liederkranz and two-minute 78s
summary: Basie recordings were short, with fewer solos than at the Savoy.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Speaking of that, I wanted to ask about the difference in making records when you first started out, say with Count Basie for example. Let me ask you one thing about the difference between what you would play in the studio with Count Basie and those the 78’s, the famous Decca things, “Every Tub” and all that, as opposed to what you were doing in live performances. How much different were the things we hear now that people study and emulate and musicologists are studying them as representative of the Basie band of the ‘30’s? These were very short performances by necessity and how much different were they from what you would be doing in a dance hall or nightclub at the time?

Well, most of it was prepared at a dance hall or a nightclub. Preparing for a record date, if we had some arrangements that Basie wanted to do, we’d play it on the job. When I was with the band, we would record in studios and they’d have only one microphone. So that came down right in the middle. And you could hear everybody with that one microphone in an old studio called Liederkranz in New York, that was the most popular one to record in. It was an old mansion but it had a great sound in there. So, I don’t think there’s any difference in what you would prepare for at a record date than what you would prepare for at a concert.
In those days, it couldn’t be over two minutes and, never no three minutes because you couldn’t get air time if you played it over three minutes. Now, you can play some 20 minutes on one tune.
But at the Savoy, if you played the same arrangement, would you be playing only three minutes?
Would there just be a lot more solos?

There would be less solos on the record date, but get to the dance hall, at the Savoy, like “Every Tub” or something, one of those arrangements which was two minutes and 30 seconds on the record. When we’d get to the Savoy, Basie’d say “Well, you go for yourself,” when you play now, you play four, five, whatever you want to play.
You take liberties. But you couldn’t do that at a record date.
